newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin blasts unpopular Moscow sculptor.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin blasts unpopular Moscow sculptor.

text.p: Russian President Boris Yeltsin on Friday criticised Moscow's leading monumentalist sculptor, who works have triggered a wave of discontent from a population weaned on massive Soviet art monuments of often dubious quality.
Interfax news agency said Yeltsin told Russian media chiefs that Zurab Tsereteli's monuments, including an omage to Tsar Peter the Great now in the works, were not beautifying the nation's capital.

"I recently have more than once criticised Moscow Mayor Yuri Luzhkov and sculptor Tsereteli, especially for the monument to Peter I," Yeltsin said. "Moscow's backing of Tsereteli is a vain thing. Don't we have other sculptors and artists?"
The huge statue of the tsar, holding a ship's steering wheel as a symbol of the Russian fleet he created in the 18th century, now stands amid scaffolding on the Moscow River not far from the Kremlin.
Many Muscovites say the statue is just plain ugly, and add that the capital, hundreds of kilometres (miles) from the nearest port of St. Petersburg, has no seafaring tradition.
Tsereteli has become Russia's most controversial artist after Luzhkov commissioned him to do a series of projects, including a centerpiece for a World War Two museum which opened in 1995.

But the Russian media said Luzhkov support was lessening in wake of pressure from Moscow's artists and intellectuals, who are calling on him to halt the construction under the slogan "Down with the Tsar!".
Yeltsin also said he approved of the idea of a referendum in Moscow, proposed by artists, on whether to proceed with the construction or to dismantle the sculpture.

A commission formed by artists and Moscow officials said on Friday the cost of the monument, once finished, would be 100 billion roubles ($17.5 million), while dismantling would cost 30 to 50 billion.
